note: Post-cutoff forecast items. Every first_posted date is on or after 2026-07-01 and was checked as recorded in date_source. Item texts name no theory, author, lab, dataset or journal. All items drafted from abstracts only. Abstract files live outside git tracking.

items.actual: In serial awakenings from non-REM sleep recorded with high-density EEG, reports of dreaming, compared with reports of no experience, were preceded by a shift in spectral balance (lower delta and alpha power, higher gamma-related measures) centred over posterior cortex.
items.mirror: In serial awakenings from non-REM sleep recorded with high-density EEG, reports of dreaming, compared with reports of no experience, were preceded by a shift in spectral balance (lower delta and alpha power, higher gamma-related measures) centred over prefrontal cortex.
items.bears_on: Posterior versus prefrontal location of the correlates of experience when report and responsiveness are held constant (sleep, within-state contrast).
items.key_results: 256-channel EEG in 140 participants; 699 NREM stage 2 and 3 awakenings (351 dreaming experience, 348 no experience); features from the 60 s before awakening. Dreaming went with shifts in posterior spectral balance (reduced alpha and delta power, increased gamma-related measures) and altered large-scale network organisation. Participant-level cross-validated classifiers were all above chance; best ensemble ROC-AUC 0.80. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only. The abstract says the shift was posterior but does not state a test of frontal regions; the mirror moves the location. A posterior result in this paradigm is well known from earlier work, so the direction is guessable from prior literature.
items.excluded: Pre-seal review: replicates famous item C17, which sits in the same blind packet and is recalled at 0.90-0.97, so its real side is given away.

items.actual: In a large cohort of patients with disorders of consciousness, spontaneous high-amplitude EEG slow waves were more frequent in minimally conscious patients than in unresponsive patients, and more frequent, steeper slow waves predicted better recovery at one year.
items.mirror: In a large cohort of patients with disorders of consciousness, spontaneous high-amplitude EEG slow waves were more frequent in unresponsive patients than in minimally conscious patients, and more frequent, steeper slow waves predicted poorer recovery at one year.
items.bears_on: Whether slow-wave (bistable, low-complexity) activity marks absence of consciousness or instead preserved thalamocortical networks; integration and complexity under loss of consciousness.
items.key_results: 256-channel EEG during the Local-Global paradigm in 236 patients (123 UWS, 62 MCS-, 29 MCS+). Slow waves were more frequent in MCS than UWS; slopes were steeper frontally and rose faster in patients with higher levels of consciousness or markers of conscious access. More frequent and steeper slow waves predicted recovery of consciousness and functional independence at one year. Classification AUC 0.62 and 0.71 (MCS-, MCS+ vs UWS); outcome prediction 0.56-0.58. Slow-wave occurrence was greater after traumatic than anoxic injury and scaled with integrity of subcortico-cortical fibres. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only. Associations are modest at the individual level; aetiology (traumatic vs anoxic) covaries with both slow waves and diagnosis.

items.actual: In simulated mean-field networks progressively rewired to vary the balance between integration and differentiation, complexity measured from responses to perturbation peaked at intermediate, small-world wiring, while measures computed from spontaneous activity behaved inconsistently, some tracking integration and others differentiation.
items.mirror: In simulated mean-field networks progressively rewired to vary the balance between integration and differentiation, complexity measured from spontaneous activity peaked at intermediate, small-world wiring, while measures computed from responses to perturbation behaved inconsistently, some tracking integration and others differentiation.
items.bears_on: Whether perturbational or observational complexity measures track the structural coexistence of integration and differentiation that integration-based accounts tie to consciousness.
items.key_results: Wilson-Cowan mean-field simulations over a range of architectures produced by systematic rewiring. Observational measures were heterogeneous: some sensitive mainly to integration, others to differentiation, some to neither. Perturbational measures peaked at intermediate rewiring, scaled with small-worldness, were robust to common-driver confounds, and were highest in a wake-like regime near critical instability, declining as sleep-like dynamics spread. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only. Simulation, not brain data; the result depends on the model class and the set of measures chosen.

items.actual: In rats recorded with hemisphere-wide electrocorticography, cortical states typical of deep desflurane anaesthesia showed, compared with the awake state, a weakened feedback dominance of theta-band travelling waves.
items.mirror: In rats recorded with hemisphere-wide electrocorticography, cortical states typical of deep desflurane anaesthesia showed, compared with the awake state, a preserved feedback dominance of theta-band travelling waves.
items.bears_on: Whether loss of feedback (top-down, recurrent) signalling accompanies anaesthetic unresponsiveness (recurrent-processing and workspace accounts vs accounts indifferent to direction).
items.key_results: Desflurane at 6, 4, 2 and 0%. In states mainly seen at 4-6%, delta-band travelling waves were more frequent and more stereotyped (more planar waves, fewer source/sink patterns) than awake. Theta and gamma wave rate and pattern complexity were largely unchanged, but planar-wave direction became more variable. Feedback dominance of theta diminished and feedforward dominance of gamma was attenuated. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only. Rodent ECoG; 'feedback' is defined by wave direction on the cortical surface. The mirror uses 'preserved' rather than 'strengthened'.

items.actual: In rats under deep desflurane anaesthesia, a spontaneously occurring cortical state with awake-like spectral properties, during which the animals stayed behaviourally unresponsive, showed travelling-wave dynamics that shifted partly toward those of the awake state.
items.mirror: In rats under deep desflurane anaesthesia, a spontaneously occurring cortical state with awake-like spectral properties, during which the animals stayed behaviourally unresponsive, showed travelling-wave dynamics that stayed like those of the other deep-anaesthesia states.
items.bears_on: Whether awake-like large-scale cortical dynamics can occur without behavioural responsiveness; dissociation of dynamical signatures from the behavioural state.
items.key_results: The 'paradoxical' state occurs mainly in deep anaesthesia with behavioural unresponsiveness; its travelling-wave dynamics showed partial, frequency-dependent shifts toward the awake pattern. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only. Shifts are partial and frequency-dependent; the abstract does not say which bands moved. Same paper as the previous item.

items.actual: When cortex was probed with transcranial magnetic stimulation and EEG, blind people compared with sighted controls showed stronger frontal-to-occipital effective connectivity, while occipital-to-frontal propagation was unchanged.
items.mirror: When cortex was probed with transcranial magnetic stimulation and EEG, blind people compared with sighted controls showed stronger occipital-to-frontal effective connectivity, while frontal-to-occipital propagation was unchanged.
items.bears_on: Direction of large-scale influence (top-down from frontal cortex vs bottom-up from posterior cortex) when a sensory area is repurposed; front-versus-back commitments.
items.key_results: TMS-EEG of frontal and occipital areas in 16 blind and 16 sighted participants. Occipital TMS-evoked potentials in the blind were faster and lower in amplitude, resembling frontal responses, which did not differ between groups. Source analyses showed a specific enhancement of frontal-to-occipital effective connectivity; occipital-to-frontal propagation unchanged. Faster occipital dynamics went with stronger frontal-driven occipital recruitment. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only. Small groups. The finding concerns plasticity, so its bearing on consciousness is indirect.

items.actual: Simultaneous scalp and intracranial recordings during median-nerve stimulation showed that the scalp negativity near 140 ms that has been linked to tactile awareness is the scalp manifestation of an insulo-opercular field potential that follows a sustained high-frequency response there.
items.mirror: Simultaneous scalp and intracranial recordings during median-nerve stimulation showed that the scalp negativity near 140 ms that has been linked to tactile awareness is the scalp manifestation of a primary somatosensory field potential that follows the initial phasic response there.
items.bears_on: Where an early candidate marker of sensory awareness arises: primary sensory cortex versus higher insulo-opercular cortex (early sensory and recurrent accounts vs later-stage accounts).
items.key_results: Simultaneous high-density scalp EEG and intracranial EEG. The N140 (somatosensory awareness negativity) is the scalp manifestation of the insulo-opercular local field potential that follows the tonic broadband high-frequency (50-150 Hz) response to stimulation. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only; no sample size in the abstract. The study localises the component; it does not itself contrast aware with unaware trials.

items.actual: In a visual masking task, people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, compared with healthy older adults, showed a reduced early visual awareness negativity as well as a reduced late positivity and reduced fronto-parietal activation.
items.mirror: In a visual masking task, people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, compared with healthy older adults, showed a preserved early visual awareness negativity but a reduced late positivity and reduced fronto-parietal activation.
items.bears_on: Whether early posterior and late fronto-parietal signatures of awareness dissociate when cognition and report decline (early-sensory vs late-ignition markers; report and metacognition).
items.key_results: EEG and fMRI with a visual masking paradigm and a movie task. Controls showed the expected awareness responses. In mild-moderate AD the VAN and late-positivity markers and fronto-parietal activation were significantly reduced. In severe, minimally responsive AD there was limited evidence of fronto-parietal markers, which may reflect attentional and task insensitivity. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only; sample sizes not given. Reduced markers could reflect attention or task engagement, not awareness. The mirror keeps the late reduction and flips only the early component.

items.actual: In healthy adults, low-intensity focused ultrasound aimed at the thalamus changed how long people took to report their subjective visual experience, depending on target and pulsing pattern, but did not change how long they took to categorise the stimulus.
items.mirror: In healthy adults, low-intensity focused ultrasound aimed at the thalamus changed how long people took to categorise the stimulus, depending on target and pulsing pattern, but did not change how long they took to report their subjective visual experience.
items.bears_on: Whether thalamic modulation acts on first-order visual processing or on the later stage of subjective report (report vs no-report, higher-order and access accounts vs sensory accounts).
items.key_results: 60 adults randomised to 70% or 5% duty cycle, four left thalamic targets. A target-by-duty-cycle interaction was found for report latency (RT2) but not categorisation latency (RT1). At the ventroposterior target, adjusted RT2 was 55.9 ms longer under 70% than 5%. More anterior focal spots shortened RT2 under 70% and lengthened it under 5%. Intensity-RT2 correlations differed by duty cycle in 18.8% of thalamic voxels. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only. The outcome is report latency, not awareness itself; an interaction effect without a sham arm described in the abstract. Shares one co-author with the travelling-waves items, hence the shared cluster.

items.actual: When an unexpected task-irrelevant stimulus made people miss a visual or auditory probe shortly afterwards, the misses were accompanied by a late parietal positivity to the surprising stimulus that shrank over trials together with the behavioural deficit, whereas early perceptual components did not habituate.
items.mirror: When an unexpected task-irrelevant stimulus made people miss a visual or auditory probe shortly afterwards, the misses were accompanied by enlarged early perceptual components to the surprising stimulus that shrank over trials together with the behavioural deficit, whereas the late parietal positivity did not habituate.
items.bears_on: Whether failures of awareness under attentional capture arise at an early sensory stage or a late, capacity-limited stage (attention vs awareness; early vs late signatures).
items.key_results: 33 participants did visual and auditory versions with EEG. Probe detection was severely impaired only on the first few surprise trials. Deficits were accompanied by a late parietal positivity time-locked to the surprise (novelty-P3-like) that attenuated across trials with the behavioural effect. It was similar across modalities, but deficit sizes were not correlated across modalities and surprises in one modality did not reduce effects in the other. Probe-evoked and early perceptual components differed by modality and did not habituate. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only (paywalled). The positivity is locked to the surprise stimulus, not to seen versus missed probes; few miss trials per person.

items.date_source: Crossref api.crossref.org/works/<DOI> (published-online and created 2026-07-22); Europe PMC firstPublicationDate agrees where indexed; preprint check: title search found only an unrelated-group 2024 preprint on the same question; author-name search uninformative (common surnames)
items.actual: With EEG frequency tagging of a stream of made-up three-syllable words, neural tracking of the hidden word structure was present in healthy controls and minimally conscious patients but was not significant in patients with unresponsive wakefulness syndrome.
items.mirror: With EEG frequency tagging of a stream of made-up three-syllable words, neural tracking of the hidden word structure was present in healthy controls and minimally conscious patients and was also significant in patients with unresponsive wakefulness syndrome.
items.bears_on: Whether extracting regularities over time needs consciousness or runs automatically without it (scope of unconscious processing; integration over time).
items.key_results: 46 patients and 25 controls. The learning effect was seen in controls and MCS; no significant effect in UWS. Stronger neural learning predicted better behavioural scores in MCS but not UWS; the effect correlated with behavioural scores and 6-month outcome in traumatic but not non-traumatic patients. EEG models separated controls from patients and MCS from UWS. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only. A null in the unresponsive group may be a power issue; group sizes per diagnosis not in the abstract. A different group posted a preprint on the same question in 2024, so the direction may be guessable. Preprint check for this paper is weaker than for the others.

items.date_source: Crossref api.crossref.org/works/<DOI> (published-online 2026-09-04, created 2026-09-05); Europe PMC firstPublicationDate agrees where indexed; preprint check: no matching preprint in Crossref posted-content title search or Europe PMC author search
items.actual: In a placebo-controlled crossover study, psilocybin acutely lowered alpha and beta power and raised the diversity of the gamma-band EEG signal, and people with larger rises in diversity reported stronger acute psychological effects.
items.mirror: In a placebo-controlled crossover study, psilocybin acutely lowered alpha and beta power and lowered the diversity of the gamma-band EEG signal, and people with larger falls in diversity reported stronger acute psychological effects.
items.bears_on: Whether signal diversity (differentiation, complexity) rises with the intensity of altered experience (complexity and integration accounts; prediction-relaxation accounts).
items.key_results: Double-blind crossover, N = 20, about 0.26 mg/kg; high-density resting EEG at baseline, 1, 3, 6 and 24 h. Alpha/beta power fell and gamma-band signal diversity rose at 1-3 h, back to baseline at 6 h. Gamma diversity correlated with acute psychological effects (r = 0.71); largest rises in those with lower baseline complexity. At 24 h, reduced delta/theta power correlated with positive life changes at 4 weeks (r = -0.47 to -0.57). (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only. Rises in diversity under psychedelics are a known pattern, so the direction is guessable from earlier work; diversity change may partly follow the spectral change.

items.actual: In large language models, the representations a model is poised to put into words carried coherent content only in an intermediate band of layers, and the model's weights broadcast them more widely than other representations.
items.mirror: In large language models, the representations a model is poised to put into words carried coherent content across nearly all layers, and the model's weights broadcast them no more widely than other representations.
items.bears_on: Whether a capacity-limited, widely broadcast workspace-like structure emerges in an artificial system (workspace-like structure in AI; substrate-dependent accounts would not credit it).
items.key_results: A new interpretability method identifies the representations a model is poised to verbalise. They carry coherent content only in an intermediate band of layers, hold on the order of tens of concepts at a time and are broadcast by the weights more widely than other representations. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only. The mirror flips three properties at once. The abstract's own framing names a theory; the item text does not.
items.edit_note: Coordinator edit before sealing: dropped the 'tens vs thousands of concepts' clause (implausible on the mirror side).

items.date_source: arXiv API export.arxiv.org/api/query?id_list=<id>v1, published date of v1
items.actual: In large language models, the representations a model is poised to put into words were used to carry the intermediate steps of silent reasoning, while automatic processing such as text parsing and routine inference proceeded without them.
items.mirror: In large language models, the representations a model is poised to put into words were used to carry automatic processing such as text parsing and routine inference, while the intermediate steps of silent reasoning proceeded without them.
items.bears_on: Whether an artificial system shows a functional split between reportable, flexibly usable contents and automatic processing (access and workspace accounts; attention and higher-order accounts).
items.key_results: The verbalisable representations can be reported, deliberately summoned and held, used to carry intermediate steps of silent reasoning, and passed as arguments to downstream computations, while automatic processing such as text parsing and routine inference proceeds without them. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only; the abstract gives no quantities for the split. Same paper as the previous item.
items.edit_note: Coordinator edit before sealing: mirror rewritten as a clean swap of the two roles.

items.date_source: arXiv API export.arxiv.org/api/query?id_list=<id>v1, published date of v1
items.actual: When language models that reuse the same weights across depth (looped, recurrent transformers) were tested with the suite used on a standard feedforward model, verbalisable, causally potent representations formed in the recurrent part of each architecture.
items.mirror: When language models that reuse the same weights across depth (looped, recurrent transformers) were tested with the suite used on a standard feedforward model, verbalisable, causally potent representations did not form in the recurrent part of either architecture.
items.bears_on: Whether workspace-like structure in AI survives when depth is implemented by recurrence rather than a feedforward stack (recurrent vs feedforward; workspace-like structure in AI).
items.key_results: Two iterated models (48 layers looped 4 times; a 4-layer core recurred 16 times) against a 64-layer untied baseline, with lens fitting, readout and eleven causal experiment families. A workspace forms in the iterated part of each architecture, but recurrence changes access: one model rebuilds content every loop and linear transport cannot carry it across loop boundaries; the other carries content across all recurrences but reads, writes and ablations act within a window of about two recurrences. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only. Depends on the earlier feedforward result (previous two items) but is from different authors, so a separate cluster.
items.edit_note: Pre-seal review: removed 'a band of', which presupposed N13's real side; clustered with N13/N14 (same suite).

items.date_source: Crossref api.crossref.org/works/<DOI> (created 2026-08-12; print issue 2026-09); Europe PMC firstPublicationDate agrees where indexed; preprint check: no preprint found by Crossref posted-content title search or Europe PMC author search
items.actual: In placebo-controlled crossover experiments with transcranial magnetic stimulation and EEG in healthy people, the benzodiazepine alprazolam reduced perturbational complexity in the late response window, whereas the sedative zolpidem did not change it.
items.mirror: In placebo-controlled crossover experiments with transcranial magnetic stimulation and EEG in healthy people, the sedative zolpidem reduced perturbational complexity in the late response window, whereas the benzodiazepine alprazolam did not change it.
items.bears_on: Whether perturbational complexity moves with sedative drug action in people who are not unconscious, and which inhibitory mechanism drives it (integration and complexity measures).
items.key_results: Alprazolam decreased beta-band phase coupling in the early feedforward stage and, in the late recurrent stage, reduced significant current density, current scattering and PCI-lz. Zolpidem increased early current density and spectral perturbations but did not affect phase coupling, scattering or PCI-lz. Early phase-coupling changes predicted the late changes and a sedation marker. Diazepam replicated the alprazolam effects. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only (paywalled); sample sizes and doses not in the abstract. Theory relevance is weaker than for other items: the contrast is between two drugs of one class, and a rater needs pharmacology more than a theory of consciousness to pick a side.

items.actual: Across fMRI datasets, closed-loop connectivity motifs among thalamic nuclei increased during non-REM sleep stages 2 and 3, but no such increase was seen during propofol anaesthesia or in unresponsive wakefulness syndrome.
items.mirror: Across fMRI datasets, closed-loop connectivity motifs among thalamic nuclei increased during non-REM sleep stages 2 and 3, and the same increase was seen during propofol anaesthesia and in unresponsive wakefulness syndrome.
items.bears_on: Whether different unresponsive states share one subcortical signature or differ in thalamic organisation (state-general vs state-specific accounts of loss of consciousness).
items.key_results: Six fMRI and EEG datasets across sleep, propofol anaesthesia and UWS. In N2 and N3, centromedian and ventral posterolateral nuclei showed convergent edge-community profiles and more closed-loop intra-thalamic motifs, not seen in anaesthesia or UWS. In N3, directed connectivity along centromedian to ventral posterolateral to pulvinar increased; stronger connectivity covaried with N3 delta power, which was higher before awakening and associated with three-month improvement in UWS. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only. Thalamic nuclei are small for fMRI; most theories of consciousness say little about intra-thalamic motifs, so ratings may sit near even.

items.actual: In a meta-analysis of several hundred neuroimaging studies of self-related processing sorted into ten forms of self, no single brain location was significant across all ten maps; each form occupied different parts of the cortical midline and insula.
items.mirror: In a meta-analysis of several hundred neuroimaging studies of self-related processing sorted into ten forms of self, one shared set of midline and insular locations was significant across all ten maps; the forms differed mainly outside that common core.
items.bears_on: Whether self-related processing has a single neural core or is a shifting set of distributed systems (self-model, higher-order and attention-schema commitments about a unified self-representation).
items.key_results: 912 publications clustered into ten forms (e.g. autobiographical memory, body ownership, interoception). No single location was significant in all ten maps, though each occupied different parts and amounts of midline and insular territory. Patterns varied with study context and resembled maps of general functions. Graded combinations of patterns predicted regions in held-out publications better than single patterns or on/off combinations. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only. 'No location significant in all ten' depends on thresholds and on how the forms were clustered; bears on self more than on consciousness as such.

items.actual: In long-term meditators, deep absorptive meditation compared with eyes-open rest raised beta and gamma EEG power without changing delta, theta or alpha power, and model fits to the spectra placed the cortex in a more inhibition-dominant regime.
items.mirror: In long-term meditators, deep absorptive meditation compared with eyes-open rest raised delta, theta and alpha EEG power without changing beta or gamma power, and model fits to the spectra placed the cortex in a more excitation-dominant regime.
items.bears_on: What cortical regime accompanies a state of absorbed, detached awareness: fast-band activity with stronger inhibitory gain versus slow-band activity (precision and gain accounts; attention and self-model accounts).
items.key_results: 18 long-term meditators, eyes-open rest vs meditation. Higher beta1, beta2 and gamma power, no change in delta, theta or alpha, and lower beta-band temporal non-stationarity. Corticothalamic model fits showed stronger cortical inhibitory gain and lower effective intracortical gain. Model estimates related to subjective absorption, with trend-level links to dissociation. (abstract only)
items.limits: Abstract only. Small sample, frontal EEG only; gamma power during meditation can be muscle artefact; regime inferred from a model fit.
